notes.h: The land question before 1879: the 1870 Act and its limits
notes.b: Irish tenants held land on yearly or short leases, with little security, and the Land Act of 1870 did not give them the protection they wanted.
points: Most Irish tenants held land from landlords on short or yearly tenancies, and they could be evicted if they fell behind with rent.
The Land Act 1870, passed under Gladstone’s first ministry, gave compensation for improvements made by tenants and for eviction without default.
The 1870 Act’s compensation for disturbance could be waived by landlords through contract, so many landlords avoided paying it.
The Act did not fix rents or give tenants security of tenure, which left the two main grievances of the Land League untouched.
The Land War was a response to these limits, and to the agricultural depression that followed the 1870 Act.

notes.h: The agricultural depression and the Land League (1877–1881)
notes.b: Poor harvests and falling prices from 1877 to 1879 pushed tenants into rent arrears and evictions, which gave land agitation its mass support.
points: The agricultural depression of 1877–79 combined bad harvests, including the wet summer of 1879, with falling prices for farm produce.
Michael Davitt organised the Mayo Land League at Irishtown, Co. Mayo, in 1879, and its meetings spread the call for reform across the west.
The Irish National Land League was founded in Dublin in October 1879 with Parnell as president, and it campaigned for the Three Fs: fair rent, fixity of tenure and free sale.
Local Land Leagues used rent strikes, boycotting and public meetings to press tenants to resist eviction and to pay only rents they judged fair.
Agrarian crime such as moonlighting, the night-time attacks on cattle and property, rose in the Land War and alarmed the government.

notes.b: Boycotting gave the language a new word, and the government answered the Land War with coercion.
points: Captain Charles Boycott, a land agent on the Lough Mask estate in Co. Mayo, was ostracised by tenants and labourers in 1880, and his name became a general term for social exclusion.
In the autumn of 1880 Ulster Protestant labourers were brought under police protection to harvest Boycott’s crops, which underlined how far the ostracism reached.
The Ladies’ Land League, founded in 1881 under Anna Parnell, organised relief for evicted families and ran the land campaign in some areas.
The Protection of Person and Property Act 1881, known as the Coercion Act, allowed detention without trial and was passed in March 1881.
Parnell and other League leaders were arrested in October 1881, and the League was suppressed under the coercion legislation.

notes.h: The Land Act of 1881 and the No Rent Manifesto
notes.b: The 1881 Act brought the Three Fs into law through state courts, and the League answered it with a call to withhold rent.
points: The Land Law (Ireland) Act 1881 gave tenants the Three Fs: a fair rent set by the new land courts, fixity of tenure, and the right to sell their interest in the holding.
The Act set up the Irish Land Commission and the land courts, and its fair rents were fixed for fifteen years at a time; it was passed in August 1881.
The 1881 Act created dual ownership, in which the landlord kept the freehold and the tenant held a legally protected interest in the holding.
The No Rent Manifesto of October 1881 called on tenants to withhold rent until political prisoners were released, and it was issued while the League leaders were in prison.
The Arrears Act of 1882 cleared part of the arrears of rent owed by tenants, and it was one of the concessions linked to the Kilmainham arrangement.
Land courts reduced rents substantially in many cases, though the Act’s effect was uneven and depended on tenants applying.

notes.h: The Plan of Campaign and the Conservative response (1885–1891)
notes.b: After 1885 the land struggle moved to the estate level, and Conservative governments tried to end it through land purchase and the Congested Districts Board.
points: The Plan of Campaign was launched in October 1886 as a coordinated strategy: tenants on an estate offered a reduced rent collectively, and the League supported tenants who were evicted.
The Plan of Campaign was supported by the nationalist press, including United Ireland, and William O’Brien and Timothy Harrington were among its leading promoters.
The Ashbourne Act of 1885 provided loans that covered the full purchase price, so tenants could buy their holdings from landlords.
Arthur Balfour’s Land Act of 1891 extended the purchase scheme and provided state loans for tenants to buy land.
The Congested Districts Board, set up in 1891, aimed to relieve poverty in the overcrowded western districts of Connaught, Donegal and Kerry by improving land and agriculture.
Conservative policy combined coercion with concessions, a strategy that became known as constructive unionism.

The Criminal Law and Procedure (Ireland) Act of 1887, the Crimes Act, was introduced by Arthur Balfour as Chief Secretary and made intimidation and unlawful assembly against tenancies criminal offences.
In September 1887 police fired on a crowd at Mitchelstown, Co. Cork, killing several people, an incident the nationalist press used to attack the government.
Pope Leo XIII’s rescript of 1888 condemned the Plan of Campaign and boycotting, which divided Irish Catholic opinion and weakened the League’s moral authority.

notes.h: The Land Conference, the Wyndham Act and the Birrell Act (1902–1909)
notes.b: Landlord and tenant leaders agreed to a land purchase settlement, and the state took over most of the work of buying out landlords.
points: The Land Conference of 1902–03, chaired by Lord Dunraven, brought together landlords and tenant representatives to agree a purchase scheme.
The Wyndham Land Act of 1903 gave state-funded loans to tenants to buy their farms, and landlords received a bonus of 12 per cent of the sale price.
The Wyndham Act was one of the main steps towards tenant proprietorship, and it gave landlords a financial incentive to sell.
The Labourers (Ireland) Act of 1906, also associated with George Wyndham, provided for the building of new cottages for agricultural labourers.
The Birrell Act of 1909 set up the Estates Commissioners and gave them powers to buy estates compulsorily where landlords refused to sell.
By 1914 most tenants had become owners or were in the process of buying their holdings, which ended landlordism as a political power in Ireland.

notes.b: Davitt combined physical-force Fenian background with the land campaign, and his later Labour views separated him from Parnell.
points: Born in 1846 at Straide, Co. Mayo, Davitt’s family was evicted when he was a child, an experience that shaped his commitment to the tenants’ cause.
He lost his right arm in a factory accident in Lancashire as a boy, and he worked in the mills there before joining the Fenian movement.
Davitt joined the Irish Republican Brotherhood in the 1860s and was imprisoned in 1870 for gun-running, serving seven years before his release in 1877.
As a participant, Davitt co-founded the Irish National Land League with Parnell in 1879 and was its main organiser in the west.
He was re-imprisoned in 1881 and released in 1882, and his prison writings were published as Leaves from a Prison Diary in 1885.
Contemporaries disagreed about him: unionists and many Liberals regarded him as a dangerous agitator, while tenants and many nationalists saw him as the champion of the land cause.
In 1890, after the O’Shea divorce scandal, Davitt opposed Parnell’s continued leadership, which helped to divide the Home Rule movement.
Davitt’s later politics favoured land nationalisation and labour reform, and historians tend to see him as more radical than Parnell on the social question.
His book The Fall of Feudalism in Ireland, published in 1904, gave his account of the land struggle, and he died in 1906.

notes.b: Judgements on the land campaign divide between its success in ending landlordism and its limits as a national or social reform.
points: Achievement: the land courts, the 1903 and 1909 Acts and state loans transformed Irish agriculture into a system of owner-occupiers.
Limit: the reform was achieved by state finance, so the land agitation’s radical goal of land nationalisation was not adopted.
Contemporary Liberals saw the reforms as a means of ending agrarian conflict, while nationalists saw them as the result of pressure from the Land League and the Plan of Campaign.

Historians differ on the Land War: some see it as a successful combination of mass protest and parliamentary pressure, others as a movement that depended on Parnell’s control and then fell apart after 1882.
The Plan of Campaign is judged both as an effective means of defeating evictions and as a source of division among tenants between those who joined and those who paid their rent.

Contemporary unionists and the Conservative government judged the land reforms a victory for the state over agitation, while Davitt’s followers judged them a partial answer to a land question that needed nationalisation.

keyTerms.definition: Organised public pressure for change, such as meetings, boycotts, rent campaigns and parliamentary tactics, used to press the land question.
The Land League programme of fair rent, fixity of tenure and free sale of a tenant’s interest in the holding.
The period of mass agitation from 1879 to 1882, marked by rent strikes, boycotting, evictions and agrarian crime.
The social and economic exclusion of a person who was regarded as an enemy of the tenants’ cause, named after Captain Charles Boycott in 1880.
The 1886 strategy of collective rent reduction on estates, backed by League funds to support tenants who were evicted.
The position reached by 1914, in which tenants bought their holdings with state loans and became owner-occupiers.
The Conservative policy of combining coercion with economic and land reforms to reduce support for Home Rule.
The Land Law (Ireland) Act that gave the Three Fs legal effect through land courts that fixed fair rents.
